Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

[{"id": "arka-v3-train-prompt-0300", "row_sha256": "5ae1702008a131158fd7f15debd22119a6d17af701f88ac4a78b0fbc4446a2f9", "mode": "/prompt", "language": "en", "context": {}, "identity": false, "mode_instructions": "Organize the supplied request into a clear prompt. Preserve scope and constraints. Do not invent context, requirements, or missing information. Do not perform the task.", "input": "hey, can you turn these notes into a clear prompt asking for useful questions for a discussion about instrument lessons at the Harbor Room Music Cooperative? this is a small independent music studio, not a school district program. it has two teaching rooms and three instructors, and lessons are offered in violin, piano, and guitar. the current term runs for twelve weeks, from september 9 through november 30. most students are between eight and sixteen, and there are also four adult beginners. lessons happen on weeknights, with a few Saturday appointments. I want the questions to help people talk together, not to make a decision for them or settle disagreements.

the discussion would include the instructors, families, and the studio coordinator. they have not all had the same experience, so questions should leave room for different views. some families have been at the cooperative for several terms, while a few students are in their first term. the instructors have different teaching styles, and the notes don't say that one style works better than another. please don't treat every family as having the same schedule or the same goals. One parent said, “we love that she can bring the violin home, but finding a quiet place to practice is harder than we expected.” that is one person's comment, not a finding about everyone.

it would be useful to ask about how the lesson routine is going. each weekly lesson is thirty minutes. students are expected to bring their instrument and music, but the studio keeps a spare violin and a keyboard available during lessons. the guitar instructor sometimes asks students to tune before they begin, while the piano students use the studio piano. lesson notes are sent home on paper, and families don't all read them at the same time. not sure everyone knows what to do with the notes between lessons. don't assume a missed practice means a student isn't interested. ask questions that can bring out what makes it easy or difficult to prepare, arrive, and get started, without putting any one student on the spot.

also the practice conversation matters. the coordinator says students are encouraged to practice at home, but there is no required number of minutes and no practice log. a couple of families have asked how often to practice; another family has said their evenings are already crowded. one student practices with a grandparent on sundays, and another usually practices alone after school. these are examples, not necessarily typical. Questions could help people describe what support feels useful and what feels like pressure, and ask how instructors and families can talk about practice when it isn't happening regularly. don't turn that into a recommendation or a rule.

there are some access and scheduling things worth discussing too. weeknight appointments start at 4:00 and the final slot starts at 7:00. the Saturday appointments are limited, and there is no online lesson option in the current notes. two families rely on the same car, and one instructor said, “the 5:30 slot fills first.” nobody has said whether that is a problem for the whole studio. ask about how lesson times fit around school, work, transport, and other commitments, but don't suggest new hours or claim the studio can offer options that aren't listed here. include a question about what people would want the coordinator to understand about scheduling, not just whether the current times suit them.

money and materials are also part of the conversation, but handle that carefully. the term fee is paid in two installments. instrument rental is separate, and the notes don't give the rental price. families buy or borrow music books; the cooperative has a small shelf of donated books, but it may not have the title a student needs. no scholarship policy is described here, so don't imply there is one. useful questions could let people explain which costs or materials are unclear and when they find out what is needed. don't ask anyone to disclose personal finances in front of the group.

there's a small end-of-term sharing session planned for november 30. taking part is optional, and students can play alone or with another student if they want to. the notes don't say how many will take part or what pieces they are preparing. one instructor called it “a chance to show what we've been working on,” while a student said they might rather keep learning without playing in front of people. please make space to discuss what the session means to different people, how students can feel comfortable, and whether there are questions about participation, without assuming that everyone wants to perform or that anyone has decided not to.

organize the questions into a numbered section and a few clear topic groups, rather than writing a long speech or a set of answers. make the questions open-ended and useful for a shared discussion among instructors, families, and the coordinator. cover lesson routines, practice, scheduling and access, costs and materials, and the end-of-term sharing session. Keep the tone respectful and practical. Use the details above as the basis for the prompt, including the uncertainty and the two quoted comments, but don't turn individual comments into general conclusions. The request is for discussion questions only; it isn't a request for policies, recommendations, a summary of what people think, or a decision about how the cooperative should change.", "output": "Write a set of useful, open-ended questions for a respectful discussion about instrument lessons at the Harbor Room Music Cooperative. The discussion is for instructors, families, and the studio coordinator. Its purpose is to help participants share different experiences and views, not to settle disagreements or make a decision for them. Do not provide answers, policies, recommendations, or conclusions about what the cooperative should change.

The Harbor Room Music Cooperative is a small independent music studio with two teaching rooms and three instructors. It offers violin, piano, and guitar lessons. The current twelve-week term runs from September 9 through November 30. Most students are between eight and sixteen, and there are four adult beginners. Lessons take place on weeknights, with a few Saturday appointments. Participants have varied experience: some families have attended for several terms, while some students are in their first term. The instructors have different teaching styles, and the available information does not indicate that one style works better than another. Do not assume all families have the same goals or schedules.

Organize the questions under clear topic groups in one numbered section. Use a respectful, practical tone and avoid putting any individual student or family on the spot. Include questions about the following areas:

1. **Lesson routines and preparation.** Each weekly lesson is thirty minutes. Students are expected to bring their instrument and music; a spare violin and a keyboard are available at the studio during lessons. The guitar instructor sometimes asks students to tune before starting, and piano students use the studio piano. Lesson notes are sent home on paper, but families do not all read them at the same time. It is unclear whether everyone knows how to use the notes between lessons. Ask what helps or makes it difficult to prepare, arrive, and get started. Do not assume that a student who misses practice is uninterested.

2. **Practice and support.** Students are encouraged to practice at home, but there is no required number of minutes and no practice log. Some families have asked how often students should practice; another has said evenings are already crowded. One student practices with a grandparent on Sundays, and another usually practices alone after school. These are examples, not necessarily typical experiences. Ask what kinds of support feel useful or pressuring and how families and instructors can discuss practice when it is not happening regularly. Do not turn these questions into a rule or recommendation.

3. **Scheduling and access.** Weeknight appointments start at 4:00, and the final slot starts at 7:00. Saturday appointments are limited, and no online lesson option is mentioned. Two families rely on the same car. An instructor said, “the 5:30 slot fills first,” but nobody has said whether this is a problem for the whole studio. Invite discussion of how lesson times fit around school, work, transportation, and other commitments, including what participants want the coordinator to understand about scheduling. Do not propose new hours or imply that unlisted options are available.

4. **Costs and materials.** The term fee is paid in two installments. Instrument rental is separate, but no rental price is given. Families buy or borrow music books; the cooperative has a small shelf of donated books, which may not include the title a student needs. No scholarship policy is described. Ask what costs or material needs are unclear and when families find out what is needed. Do not ask anyone to disclose personal finances in front of the group, and do not imply that a scholarship policy exists.

5. **End-of-term sharing session.** A sharing session is planned for November 30. Participation is optional, and students may play alone or with another student if they choose. The available information does not say how many students will take part or which pieces they are preparing. An instructor called it “a chance to show what we've been working on,” while one student said they might rather keep learning without playing in front of people. Ask what the session means to different participants and what might help students feel comfortable. Leave room for questions about participation without assuming everyone wants to perform or that anyone has decided not to.

Keep the questions open-ended and grounded in the information provided. Treat the quoted remarks as individual comments rather than conclusions about all families, students, or instructors."}]
